newsitem.title: CANADA: U.S. salmon fishermen arrested in Canadian waters.
newsitem.headline: U.S. salmon fishermen arrested in Canadian waters.

text.p: Four U.S. fishermen were arrested on Sunday for illegally fishing sockeye salmon in Canadian waters, and their boats, nets and catch were seized, the federal government said.

An official of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans told Reuters the Lynde E and the Wanda Mae were captured in the waters of Juan de Fuca Strait near the city of Victoria off the coast of Vancouver Island while fishing with illegal nets and without the right to fish in Canadian waters.
"The big issue is that they were fishing illegally in our waters," said Robert Martinolich, the department's director of conservation and protection for the Pacific region.

Martinolich said the four fishermen had their boats, nets and catch seized and could face up to C$100,000 (US$72,600) in fines, the loss of the seized items and imprisonment if convicted of illegal fishing.
"They will probably go before a judge tomorrow," Martinolich said, adding that officers who arrested the four men believed the American fishermen knew they were illegally fishing in Canadian waters.

The arrests came amid a dispute between Canada and the United States over salmon fishing that resulted in the blockade of an Alaskan ferry on Saturday by angry Canadian fishermen in Prince Rupert, British Columbia.

The Canadian Broadcasting Corp. reported on Sunday that the ferry operator, Alaska Marine Highway, had obtained a court order demanding the fishermen disband their blockade. It said a convoy of trucks also detained by angry fishermen had obtained a court order to allow passage through a roadblock.
CBC reported the trucks had been allowed to pass on Sunday but the blockaded ferry was still unable to leave port.
U.S. officials denied Canadian allegations on Friday that the United States was breaching an international treaty by overfishing salmon in the Pacific Ocean.
"We do not believe we are in violation of this treaty," a State Department official said.

Canada's fisheries minister, David Anderson, said Alaskan fishermen had caught about 350,000 Canada-bound sockeye salmon so far in the 1997 season -- a 300 percent increase from the average of previous years.
U.S. officials say Alaskan fishermen always catch some sockeye along with the pink salmon they are entitled to catch, because the two species run together.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said on Friday, "The ratio of pink salmon to sockeye so far this season is consistent with the ratio of every year of the last five years."
Canada and the United States have been holding sporadic talks for months on how to divide Pacific salmon stocks but failed to reach agreement before this year's season started.
